sentences.text: This predator grew to a length of roughly seven meters and likely weighed around 1.2 tons.
Its head was broad and flat on the upper surface, topped by a noticeable ridge.
The animal stood about 2.2 meters tall and possessed tiny forelimbs along with small bony ridges above the eyes.
These eye ridges were similar to those seen in Allosaurus but were smaller than those found in other members of its family.
Friedrich von Huene first gave the creature its name in 1932, with a full description following in 1933 alongside Charles Alfred Matley.
The initial study relied on three incomplete skulls discovered near Jabalpur in the Lameta Formation of Madhya Pradesh.
Unfortunately, the specific specimen chosen as the standard reference has been missing since the original work was published.
Later researchers added more bones, including a nearly complete skeleton from the Raiholi site in Gujarat.
Today, scientists place Indosuchus securely within the Abelisauridae, although it was once grouped with Allosauridae.
In 1964, Alick Walker suggested the animal belonged to the Tyrannosauridae instead.
By 1986, José Bonaparte had determined it was an abelisaurid.
A 2004 study by Novas and colleagues defined the group by the forward position of the frontonasal suture relative to the lacrimal bone.
Because only certain skull parts have been recovered, the animal's taxonomic history has been unstable.
Indosuchus inhabited India during the Late Cretaceous, specifically the Maastrichtian age, between approximately 70 and 66 million years ago.
The time range for this species is the Maastrichtian, spanning from 72.2 to 66 million years ago.
